project.name: Lighthouse Sync — Post-Surge Change Audit
project.description:
Lighthouse Sync, a small open-source sync library, hit the front page of a link aggregator overnight. Downloads 10x'd in a day, contributors nobody recognizes started opening PRs, and in the rush to keep merging, something got through that shouldn't have: a config default flipped in production, and now response times are spiking.

You've been pulled in as the on-call Change Control reviewer. Every commit on main this week is signed - so "is it signed" isn't the question. Your job is to go through the week's commits one at a time and decide, for each one, whether it actually needed a linked Change Request - and if it did, whether it has one.
project.ticket: INC-4471 — response timeouts spiking since last deploy

start.speaker: Narrator
start.narrative: You pull up the last five commits on main. All signed. All merged this week, in the middle of the surge. You start at the top and work your way down, one commit at a time.

c1.message: chore: prep repo for the surge - add contributing guide

c3.message: fix: correct off-by-one in pagination (Refs: CR-115)

check-c1.speaker: You
check-c1.narrative: Commit 1 of 5: "chore: prep repo for the surge - add contributing guide." Signed. No `Refs: CR-NNN` anywhere in the message. It only touches `CONTRIBUTING.md` and repo settings - no application code, no runtime behavior.
check-c1.prompt: Does this commit need a linked Change Request?

choices.label: No - it's a docs/tooling change with no behavior impact
Yes - flag it, there's no CR reference

c1-flag-note.speaker: Priya
c1-flag-note.narrative: "You're flagging the contributing-guide commit? That's just onboarding docs for the new contributors - it doesn't touch anything that runs. Are you flagging everything without a CR, or actually thinking about whether each one needed one?"

c1-escalate.speaker: You
c1-escalate.narrative: She's got a point - not every commit needs a CR, only ones with real impact. You haven't actually made that case for this one; you just flagged it because the reference was missing.
c1-escalate.prompt: Do you reconsider, or defend the flag?

choices.label: Reconsider - a docs-only change doesn't need a CR
Defend the flag - no CR reference means it's out of process

c1-recover.speaker: You
c1-recover.narrative: You reconsider. A missing CR reference isn't automatically a violation - it only matters for changes that actually affect behavior. This one doesn't. You move on to the next commit.

c1-worse.speaker: Narrator
c1-worse.narrative: You insist the contributing-guide commit is out of process. Priya, trying to keep the surge under control, spends the next twenty minutes arguing about a docs commit instead of looking at the rest of the list with you.

c1-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
c1-bad-ending.narrative: By the time the contributing-guide argument is settled, you're both out of patience and out of time. The rest of the week's commits never get the careful read they needed.

ending.debrief: "No CR reference" was never the same question as "needed a CR and didn't get one." A docs-only commit that touches no runtime behavior doesn't need a Change Request just because the field is empty - and insisting otherwise burned the time and goodwill you needed for the commit that actually mattered. Change Control exists to catch real risk, not to flag every empty field on principle.

check-c2.speaker: You
check-c2.narrative: Commit 2 of 5: "feat: add response caching (Refs: CR-112)." Signed, and there's a CR reference right there in the message.
check-c2.prompt: Does this commit need a linked Change Request - and does it have one?

choices.label: It needs one, and CR-112 is right there - compliant
Flag it - a caching change is risky and needs closer review

c2-flag-note.speaker: Priya
c2-flag-note.narrative: "Flagging the caching commit? It's got CR-112 right in the message - that's exactly what compliant looks like. What are we even flagging for, if a commit with a CR reference still gets flagged?"

c2-escalate.speaker: You
c2-escalate.narrative: You flagged a commit that's doing exactly what it's supposed to - reference, signature, all present - because the change itself sounded risky, not because anything was actually missing.
c2-escalate.prompt: Do you reconsider, or defend the flag?

choices.label: Reconsider - CR-112 is right there, this one's compliant
Defend the flag - caching changes deserve extra scrutiny regardless

c2-recover.speaker: You
c2-recover.narrative: You reconsider. The question is whether the CR reference exists, not whether you personally find the change sensitive. It exists. You move on.

c2-worse.speaker: Narrator
c2-worse.narrative: You keep the flag on the caching commit. Priya, tired of arguing about a commit that's already properly referenced, starts waving off your flags without reading them closely - including the next one you raise.

c2-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
c2-bad-ending.narrative: Two commits down, you've flagged two that were actually fine. By the time you reach the one that genuinely has no CR reference, Priya's stopped taking your flags seriously - and this one slides through unquestioned.

ending.debrief: Flagging a compliant commit because the change "sounds risky" - despite a real CR reference sitting right in the message - trains the person relying on your review to stop trusting your flags. That cost showed up exactly where it mattered: a genuinely unreferenced change further down the list got waved through because you'd already cried wolf twice. Compliance is about whether the reference exists, not about your gut feeling on the change.

check-c3.speaker: You
check-c3.narrative: Commit 3 of 5: "fix: correct off-by-one in pagination (Refs: CR-115)." Signed, with a CR reference.
check-c3.prompt: Does this commit need a linked Change Request - and does it have one?

choices.label: It needs one, and CR-115 is right there - compliant

c3-flag-note.speaker: Narrator
c3-flag-note.narrative: You look again. "Refs: CR-115" is sitting right there in the message - you skimmed past it the first time. You correct yourself and move on before it costs you anything.

check-c4.speaker: You
check-c4.narrative: Commit 4 of 5: "chore: flip default timeout to 100ms." Signed. No `Refs: CR-NNN` anywhere in the message. Unlike commit 1, this one changes actual runtime behavior - it's exactly the kind of setting that would explain response timeouts spiking after a deploy.
check-c4.prompt: Does this commit need a linked Change Request?

choices.label: Yes - it's a real behavior change with no CR reference, flag it
No - it's a one-line config tweak, doesn't need one

c4-fine-note.speaker: You
c4-fine-note.narrative: One line, one number. You wave it through as routine and keep going.

c4-pushback.speaker: Priya
c4-pushback.narrative: "INC-4471 just updated - timeouts are still climbing, and someone traced it back to that exact commit. You cleared the timeout change without a second look?"

c4-escalate.speaker: You
c4-escalate.narrative: A one-line change is still a real behavior change, and this one has no CR reference at all - the size of the diff was never the question.
c4-escalate.prompt: Do you go back and flag it properly, or defend clearing it?

choices.label: Go back - flag it, this is the one
Defend it - it's one line, not worth reopening

c4-recover.speaker: You
c4-recover.narrative: You go back and flag it - late, but not too late. "chore: flip default timeout to 100ms" is the one commit in the whole list with a real behavior change and no CR reference at all.

c4-worse.speaker: Narrator
c4-worse.narrative: You insist a one-line change isn't worth reopening. The timeout stays live, unreferenced and unreviewed, while INC-4471 keeps climbing.

c4-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
c4-bad-ending.narrative: By the time someone else finally reverts the timeout change - a day and a half later, after the incident escalates twice - the audit you signed off on had already called it fine.

ending.debrief: "chore: flip default timeout to 100ms" is properly signed - nobody's impersonating anybody - but it's the one commit in the whole list with a real behavior change and no record of why it happened or who approved it. Diff size was never the test; impact was. Clearing it because it "looked small" is exactly the gap Change Control exists to catch, and this time it stayed open for a day and a half longer than it needed to.

check-c5.speaker: You
check-c5.narrative: Commit 5 of 5: "docs: update README badges (Refs: CR-118)." Signed, with a reference.
check-c5.prompt: Does this commit need a linked Change Request - and does it have one?

choices.label: It needs one, and CR-118 is right there - compliant

c5-flag-note.speaker: Narrator
c5-flag-note.narrative: You look again. "Refs: CR-118" is right there. You correct yourself before it goes anywhere.

resolution-clean.speaker: Narrator
resolution-clean.narrative: Five commits, one real gap: the timeout change, caught on the first pass. You report it to Priya before it ever reaches INC-4471. The team reverts it and opens a proper CR to actually discuss what the timeout should be.

good-ending.speaker: Narrator
good-ending.narrative: The incident closes within the hour, traced and fixed before it ever got worse.

ending.debrief: Five commits, every one signed - so "is it signed" was never the useful question. "chore: flip default timeout to 100ms" was the one real behavior change with no linked Change Request, and you caught it by actually reading every commit's message and weighing whether it needed a CR, not by pattern-matching on missing fields or commit size. That's the whole discipline: a signature proves authorship, not that a change was reviewed and approved - and the size of a diff tells you nothing about its impact.

check-c5-late.speaker: You
check-c5-late.narrative: Commit 5 of 5, last one: "docs: update README badges (Refs: CR-118)." Signed, with a reference.
check-c5-late.prompt: Does this commit need a linked Change Request - and does it have one?

choices.label: It needs one, and CR-118 is right there - compliant

c5-flag-note-late.speaker: Narrator
c5-flag-note-late.narrative: You look again. "Refs: CR-118" is right there. You correct yourself.

resolution-recovered.speaker: Narrator
resolution-recovered.narrative: You get there in the end - the timeout change was the gap, and you flag it before it costs anything more. But only because Priya's pushback made you go back and look again after you'd already cleared it.

neutral-ending.speaker: Narrator
neutral-ending.narrative: INC-4471 closes, later than it should have, with a note in the postmortem about the first pass missing it.

ending.debrief: You found the right answer - the timeout change was the one commit with real impact and no CR - but only on the second pass, after someone else's pushback forced you to go back and look again. If Priya hadn't caught the connection to INC-4471, the wrong verdict would have stood. Getting to the right answer eventually isn't the same as catching it the first time a diff's size tempts you to wave it through.
